title: Summarizing Known Attacks on Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram TLS (DTLS)
summary: This informational document summarizes several serious attacks on Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram TLS (DTLS), including attacks on commonly used ciphers and modes of operation. It aims to motivate generic and protocol-specific recommendations for using TLS and DTLS safely.

plainLanguage.summary: Over the years, people found clever ways to break the secret-keeping system websites use. This note collects those tricks in one place so everyone can learn from them.

questions: what are the known attacks on tls

subtitle: A snapshot of the serious attacks on TLS and DTLS that motivated the recommendations for using them safely.

tldr.problem: Over a few years, several major attacks hit TLS, including attacks on its most common ciphers and modes, AES-CBC and RC4, which together make up most usage.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the attacks that motivated the recommendations of the UTA working group, from SSL stripping and BEAST to padding oracles, RC4 biases, compression attacks, renegotiation flaws and implementation bugs, with mitigations where known.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational snapshot, not a standard. It reflects knowledge at the time of writing, and says new attacks will likely be found.

today: RFC 7457 is an Informational RFC and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. The RFC itself calls its list a snapshot in time as of February 2015, so it does not cover attacks found afterwards.

sections.title: Why a List of Attacks
sections.content:
RFC 7457 summarizes several serious attacks on TLS. Its quick summary is that both AES-CBC and RC4, which together make up most current usage, have been seriously attacked in the context of TLS. This was one motivation for the UTA working group, which was tasked with generic and protocol-specific recommendations for the use of TLS and DTLS.

The list is not an extensive survey. The RFC quotes the saying that attacks always get better and never get worse, so the document is only a snapshot in time. Where an attack has a CVE identifier, the RFC gives it. Unless Section 3 says otherwise, everything in the document also applies to DTLS.
sections.plainLanguage: People keep finding new ways to break the secret code websites use. This note records the known tricks so that better advice can be written.

sections.title: Downgrade, Padding and Cipher Attacks
sections.content:
SSL stripping removes TLS altogether by modifying unencrypted traffic that asks for it. It only works if the client first uses plain HTTP, and HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) is a common mitigation. STARTTLS has similar downgrade problems, plus a command injection flaw in applications that kept pipelined commands in a buffer across the TLS upgrade; the fix is to require the input buffer to be empty before negotiating TLS.

BEAST exploits the predictable initialization vector of CBC in TLS 1.0 to decrypt parts of a packet, such as HTTP cookies. The MAC-then-encrypt design in all current TLS versions allows padding oracle attacks. Lucky Thirteen is a timing side channel, and can be mitigated by authenticated encryption such as AES-GCM or encrypt-then-MAC. POODLE, a variant against SSL 3.0 that does not use timing, has no known mitigation.

RC4 has long-known weaknesses, and recent cryptanalysis of keystream biases needs 2^26 sessions or 13x2^30 encryptions, so RC4 can no longer be seen as providing sufficient security for TLS. CRIME abuses TLS-level compression to decrypt cookies, while TIME and BREACH use HTTP-level compression. Disabling TLS compression mitigates TIME, but there is no TLS-level mitigation for BREACH, so application-level fixes are needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers can trick you into a lock-free door, guess secrets by watching how the lock reacts, or exploit weak old locks. Some tricks have fixes and some do not.

sections.title: Keys, Certificates and Handshakes
sections.content:
TLS used with RSA certificates has been hit by practical attacks such as Bleichenbacher and Klima. Bleichenbacher is mitigated in TLS 1.0, while Klima, which relies on a version-check oracle, is only mitigated by TLS 1.1. RSA also often has exploitable timing issues unless the implementation takes care to eliminate them. A certificate fuzzing tool found many validation vulnerabilities in TLS libraries.

With most non-Diffie-Hellman cipher suites, getting the server's private key is enough to decrypt any session, past and future. The RFC says stolen keys have been used for large-scale monitoring. Protecting the key helps, and forward secrecy is more effective. For Diffie-Hellman, using predefined groups mitigates a cross-protocol attack, and clients that do not verify the received parameters are exposed to man-in-the-middle attacks, because TLS does not mandate that check.

The renegotiation attack applies to all current versions and is resolved by the extension in RFC 5746. The triple handshake attack lets an attacker make two TLS connections share keying material, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks and breaking safe renegotiation and channel binding.
sections.plainLanguage: If a thief steals the master key, every past and future message can be read, unless each conversation used its own one-time key. Some tricks also fool two parties into sharing one secret by mistake.

sections.title: Hosts, Denial of Service and Implementations
sections.content:
Virtual host confusion abuses SSLv3 fallback and badly handled server session caches to connect to a different virtual host than the one the server intended. Denial of service is a risk because a client can force the server to do relatively large computational work with little effort of its own.

Even a well-specified protocol can be implemented badly. The RFC lists implementations that omit certificate validation, fail to check the server identity against the Subject Alternative Name field, or validate the chain incorrectly or with an outdated trust anchor list. It also cites Heartbleed, which came from a simple bounds-check mistake and affected a wide swath of the Internet when discovered in April 2014.

Usability matters too. Users are used to clicking through invalid certificate warnings, which both legitimate SSL proxies and attackers rely on. The RFC says mitigation is complex and will probably combine protocol mechanisms such as HSTS and certificate pinning with careful UI design.
sections.plainLanguage: Even a great lock fails if the builder forgets to check the key, or if people always click "yes, open the door" when asked.

sections.title: Applicability to DTLS
sections.content:
DTLS is an adaptation of TLS for UDP. For the attacks in this document, DTLS 1.0 is equivalent to TLS 1.1, with the single exception of RC4, which is disallowed in DTLS. DTLS 1.2 is equivalent to TLS 1.2.

The security considerations section notes that the document describes attacks informationally and has no security implications by itself, while its companion documents, especially the recommendations draft, do.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS is TLS for a different kind of delivery. It has the same weak spots, except one old trick that is simply not allowed.
